Q008705:
## The streaming analytics pattern
A common Google Cloud design for streaming analytics follows the data supply chain:
- **Collect and ingest**: Pub/Sub receives events from many devices and holds them for consumers.
- **Process**: Dataflow reads the stream, cleans, deduplicates and aggregates it.
- **Store and analyze**: BigQuery stores the results and answers SQL questions.
- **Activate and visualize**: Looker presents dashboards and reports to the business.
Each product does one job well, and the managed services scale without servers to run.
## Reading the options
Only one sequence gives each service the role it actually has.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Pub/Sub, Dataflow, BigQuery, Looker (correct):** ingestion, transformation, storage and analysis, and visualization are each handled by the service designed for that stage.
- ✗ **B. Looker first:** Looker is a presentation layer and cannot receive device readings, and BigQuery and Dataflow are also swapped into the wrong roles.
- ✗ **C. BigQuery receiving:** BigQuery stores and analyzes, Dataflow transforms, and Pub/Sub moves messages; here every role is reassigned incorrectly.
- ✗ **D. Dataflow receiving:** Dataflow processes data and Pub/Sub carries messages, so this reverses their jobs, and Looker does not clean data.

## Key idea
Streaming analytics chain: Pub/Sub ingests, Dataflow processes, BigQuery stores and analyzes, Looker presents.
Q008706:
## Strategic factors when choosing an AI approach
A leader weighs a few factors before picking how to get an AI capability:
- **Speed**: how soon the business needs it.
- **Development effort**: how much building, data preparation and maintenance the team must do.
- **Differentiation**: whether the capability is a source of competitive advantage or a commodity.
- **Technical expertise**: whether the organization has people who can build and run models.
- **Choice and flexibility**: whether the approach lets the business change models or tools later.
## The spectrum on Google Cloud
Ready-made, pre-trained APIs (Vision, Translation, Speech-to-Text) are fastest and need the least expertise. Foundation models such as Gemini can be prompted or tuned. AutoML and custom training on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) give more differentiation at the cost of more data, time and skill.
## Reading the scenario
Short deadline, no ML staff, common task, no differentiation: every factor points to the pre-trained API end of the spectrum.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom model from scratch:** it maximizes effort and time for a task that is not a differentiator, and a pre-trained API is not inherently less accurate.
- ✗ **B. Research team first:** designing a new architecture is the slowest, most expertise-heavy path and ignores the deadline.
- ✗ **C. Multi-year in-house platform:** it misses the busy season and invests heavily in a commodity capability.
- ✓ **D. Pre-trained speech API (correct):** transcription is a standard task that Speech-to-Text already does, so the insurer meets the six-week date without ML staff or training data.

## Key idea
Common task plus tight deadline plus no ML skills = start with a pre-trained API.
Q008707:
## Differentiation is the reason to build
A pre-trained API is trained by Google on broad data and is available to everyone, so it cannot encode what is unique to your business. When the capability is the product or the edge, the unique asset is your own data, and a model trained or tuned on it can produce results competitors cannot buy.
## What you pay for it
Custom models cost more time, data preparation and skill than calling an API. That is why the choice is a trade-off: build when differentiation justifies the effort, buy when the task is common.
## Reading the scenario
Fifteen years of proprietary history and a willingness to wait make differentiation the deciding factor.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Less expertise:** custom work needs data preparation and evaluation; lower expertise is a reason to prefer ready-made services or AutoML.
- ✗ **B. Speed:** custom training takes longer than calling an existing API; the lender is accepting that cost, not avoiding it.
- ✓ **C. Differentiation (correct):** a model trained on the lender's own repayment history can learn patterns specific to its customers that no shared, generic service contains.
- ✗ **D. Uniformity:** sameness of output is the problem a differentiating model avoids, not a benefit the lender wants.

## Key idea
Proprietary data and a need to stand out favour custom models; speed and low effort favour ready-made services.
Q008708:

Tabular records, a standard prediction goal and no coding staff match AutoML. The other products solve other problems.

Standard prediction goal, labelled data, no ML coders = AutoML on Agent Platform.
Q008709:

SQL-skilled analysts with data in BigQuery = BigQuery ML.
Q008710:

Written content for global audiences with minimal effort = Cloud Translation.
Q008712:

Q008713:
## Foundation models versus task-specific APIs

Text question plus a photo plus a drafted reply is a mixed-input, generate-text job: that is a multimodal foundation model.

Mixed inputs and open-ended generation = multimodal foundation model (Gemini).

Q008719:

Q008720:

Q008728:
## Microservices and the business
In a **monolith** all features ship as one unit. In a **microservices** architecture the application is split into small services, each with one job and its own release cycle, connected by APIs.
## Business value
- **Speed**: a small change means releasing one service, not the whole system.
- **Resilience**: a fault in one service can be contained instead of taking down everything.
- **Targeted scaling**: only the busy service gets more capacity, which helps cost.
- **Team autonomy**: teams own services and change them independently.
## Trade-off
More services mean more moving parts to monitor and manage, which is why managed services and platforms such as GKE and Cloud Run are used to carry that load.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single deployable unit:** that describes the monolith the airline wants to leave, where every change needs a full release and one fault can affect everything.
- ✓ **B. Independent release and scaling (correct):** each capability ships on its own schedule and failures are contained, which directly answers the twice-a-year release problem.
- ✗ **C. One team owns everything:** microservices usually let several teams own services independently; one team owning all of them recreates the bottleneck.
- ✗ **D. No compute needed:** every service still runs on compute, whether VMs, containers or serverless; microservices change structure, not the need for compute.

## Key idea
Microservices = independent release, scaling and fault isolation, at the cost of more components to manage.

- **API products**: Apigee lets you bundle APIs or resources into a logical unit aimed at one use case for a developer, for example a "tracking" package.
- **Developer portals**: publish API products where partners can learn, register and get started.
- **Rate plans (monetization)**: define how usage is billed, the payment model or revenue share.
- **Analytics**: see which products and partners drive usage.
## Business value
The firm sells existing capabilities repeatedly through a controlled channel, without custom deals for each partner.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model-selling:** Apigee manages and monetizes APIs; it does not build a gen AI model from tracking data and sell it.
- ✓ **B. Rate plans (correct):** they define billing, payment model or revenue share, which is how usage becomes revenue.
- ✗ **C. Replacing partner apps:** monetization depends on partners using the APIs, so removing partner developers works against it.
- ✗ **D. Hosting trucks on VMs:** trucks are physical assets, and hosting infrastructure is unrelated to packaging and billing APIs.
- ✓ **E. API products and developer portal (correct):** bundling APIs into products and publishing them in a portal lets partners discover and onboard themselves.

## Key idea
Monetizing APIs = API products in a developer portal plus rate plans for billing and revenue share.
Q008746:
## Decoupling consumers from the backend
Apigee provides an API proxy layer between backend services and clients. Policies and behavior live on the proxy, so the interface the client sees can stay consistent while the service behind it changes.
## Business value for modernization
- **Gradual change**: legacy pieces can be swapped for microservices step by step, behind the same API.
- **Lower risk**: no coordinated change across dozens of apps.
- **Continuity for partners**: they keep integrating against a stable contract.
- **Works across environments**: Apigee can front services in Google Cloud, on-premises or other clouds (Apigee hybrid runs the runtime in the customer's own environment).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Consumers rewritten each time:** that is what happens with direct integrations; the proxy shields consumers from internal details.
- ✗ **B. One-weekend cutover:** the proxy layer exists to avoid big-bang changes by hiding backend changes from callers.
- ✗ **C. Backend unnecessary:** the proxy forwards and governs requests to services; the backend still does the actual work.
- ✓ **D. A stable proxy in front of a changing backend (correct):** callers keep using the same API while modernization proceeds behind it.

## Key idea
API management decouples consumers from backends, so systems can be modernized without breaking callers.
Q008747:
## Distributed denial of service (DDoS)
A **DDoS attack** tries to make a service unusable by overwhelming it with traffic or requests from many sources at once, often thousands of compromised devices called a botnet. The goal is rarely to steal data. The goal is to stop legitimate customers from getting through.
This definition is the generic industry meaning; Google Cloud's security pages simply list DDoS among the standard risks that cloud security has to address.
## Business implication
- Lost sales and a damaged reputation while the site is down.
- Contractual penalties if an availability commitment is missed.
- The loss is of **availability**, one of the three properties of the confidentiality, integrity, availability model.
## Reading the scenario
Millions of requests from many devices, an outage, and nothing copied or changed: that is a flood against availability.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. DDoS attack (correct):** traffic from many compromised sources swamped the site so real buyers could not reach it, which is a loss of availability with no data touched.
- ✗ **B. Phishing:** phishing deceives people into giving away credentials, and there is no sign of any employee being tricked or any account being accessed.
- ✗ **C. Ransomware:** ransomware locks or encrypts files and demands payment, but here nothing was encrypted and the site simply could not handle the flood of requests.
- ✗ **D. Cryptomining:** mining abuses compute capacity quietly for profit, whereas this event was a visible, short outage caused by incoming traffic.

## Key idea
DDoS = a flood of traffic from many sources that attacks availability, not data.
Q008748:
## Ransomware
**Ransomware** is malware that encrypts or locks an organization's data or systems and demands payment for restoring access. Many attackers also steal a copy of the data first and threaten to publish it.
This is the generic industry definition.
## Business implications
- **Downtime**: production, ordering or patient care may stop.
- **Data exposure**: stolen data creates regulatory and reputational risk.
- **Hard decisions**: paying does not guarantee recovery and may encourage more attacks.
- **Preparation matters**: tested, isolated backups and a recovery plan reduce the leverage an attacker has. This is the idea behind cyber resilience.
## Reading the scenario
A CFO needs the money and continuity view: stopped operations, possible exposure and the value of being able to recover without paying.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Unexpected invoice:** surprise bills are typical of cryptomining abuse, not of ransomware, whose cost is downtime and ransom.
- ✗ **B. Attacker's own systems:** ransomware runs on the victim's systems, so the exposure is to the company itself and not a traffic increase.
- ✓ **C. Halted operations and possible exposure (correct):** locked files stop work and stolen copies create further risk, so the recovery capability has to exist before the incident.
- ✗ **D. Website only:** a public web outage describes a DDoS pattern, while ransomware makes the company's own files unreadable.

## Key idea
Ransomware locks data and demands payment, so the business impact is downtime and exposure unless recovery is planned.
Q008749:
## Cryptomining abuse
In a **cryptomining** attack, someone gains access to cloud resources, often through leaked keys or weak credentials, and starts compute-heavy machines that mine cryptocurrency. The victim pays for the capacity and the attacker keeps the proceeds.
This is the generic industry definition. Google's cloud security page does note that mismanaged permission controls are a common misconfiguration.
## Business implications
- Surprise cost.
- Evidence that credentials or permissions were not well protected.
- A prompt to rotate keys, restrict who can create resources and monitor unusual activity.
## Reading the scenario
Unknown, fully loaded large machines in an unknown project, started with a leaked key, show someone is using the start-up's compute for their own gain.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Cryptomining (correct):** the leaked key let the attacker launch heavy compute for mining, which explains both the full CPU and the unexpected bill.
- ✗ **B. Hardware failure:** provider hardware problems do not launch new customer machines, and the customer is not billed for machines it did not request because of them.
- ✗ **C. DDoS:** a flood would target the start-up's own site and cause an outage, not create new machines in an unknown project.
- ✗ **D. Phishing:** phishing is a way to steal credentials, but the scenario names a leaked developer key, and the bill comes from the machines the attacker later started.

## Key idea
Cryptomining = stolen access used to run compute for the attacker, shown by an unexpected bill.
Q008750:
## Two different attack types
- **Phishing** targets people. A message, often an email, text or fake web page, pretends to come from a trusted party and persuades the recipient to share credentials, click a link or open an attachment.
- **Malware** is a broad term for malicious software: viruses, worms, ransomware, spyware and others. A **virus** is one kind that attaches itself to other files or programs and spreads when they run.
## Why they connect
Phishing is often the delivery method. A user clicks a link in a fake message and malware is installed, or enters a password into a fake login page.
These definitions are the generic industry meanings; Google's cloud security page lists phishing and malware among the common risks.
## Defences at business level
Training, multi-factor authentication and email filtering reduce phishing; updated software and endpoint protection reduce malware.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. File encryption and key:** encrypting files for payment is ransomware, a kind of malware, and attackers do not send keys by email as a definition of malware.
- ✓ **B. Deceptive message and harmful software (correct):** phishing manipulates a person, while malware is a program designed to damage or misuse systems, and the two are often linked.
- ✗ **C. Traffic flood and install policy:** a traffic flood is a DDoS attack, and malware is software, not a policy.
- ✗ **D. Self-copying code and password request:** the descriptions are swapped, because self-replicating code is a virus (one kind of malware) and the password-asking message is phishing.

## Key idea
Phishing tricks people; malware (including viruses and ransomware) is harmful software.
Q008751:
## Misconfiguration
A **misconfiguration** is a setting that leaves a resource less protected than intended, such as a public bucket, a default password, encryption left off, or permissions that are too broad. Google's cloud security guidance describes misconfiguration as one of the leading causes of data breaches in cloud environments.
## Who is responsible
Under the shared responsibility model, Google secures the underlying infrastructure, and the customer decides how its own resources are configured and who can access its data. Cloud services make sharing easy, so a careless choice has wide effect.
## Business implication
Reduce the risk with guardrails (organization policies, automated posture checks), least-privilege access, and review of settings before launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zero-day exploit:** nothing was exploited, because the data was simply reachable by anyone due to its access setting.
- ✗ **B. Provider data center:** the bucket's access setting is the customer's choice, and physical security of the facility was not involved.
- ✗ **C. Cannot be protected:** the cloud offers strong controls, and this incident was caused by a setting, not an unavoidable limit of the cloud.
- ✓ **D. Customer responsibility (correct):** configuration and access for the customer's own resources belong to the customer, so it must set and check them.
- ✓ **E. Misconfiguration (correct):** the open bucket is a setting error with no break-in needed, and this is the failure type Google names among leading causes of cloud breaches.

## Key idea
Misconfiguration (an open bucket, a default password) is a customer-side error and a leading cause of cloud breaches.
Q008752:
## Third-party risk
Attackers often go after the weakest link: a supplier, agency or partner that has trusted access to a target. If that partner is poorly secured, the attacker can arrive through the approved connection. The exam guide lists unsecured third-party systems as a threat to recognise.
## Business implications
- The company is accountable for its customers' data even when the weakness is in a partner.
- Contracts and audits must cover partner security.
## Sensible responses
- Give partners only the access they need (least privilege), and for a limited time.
- Do not treat a partner connection as automatically trusted, which is the zero-trust idea.
- Review partner security as part of supplier management.
## Reading the scenario
Nothing was wrong at the bank. The entry point was a partner with a trusted link.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Unsecured third-party system (correct):** the breach came through a partner, so the bank should restrict what partners can reach and check how well they protect their own systems.
- ✗ **B. Phishing:** phishing may have helped the attacker at the agency, but the business lesson is the unsecured partner link, and a different email vendor does not address it.
- ✗ **C. Physical damage:** the loss came from a stolen-data intrusion through a partner, and a second building would not reduce that exposure.
- ✗ **D. DDoS:** this was not a flood of traffic and no outage occurred, so more bandwidth would not have stopped data theft.

## Key idea
A partner with weak security and trusted access is a third-party risk; limit and review that access.
Q008753:
## Physical damage as a security and resilience risk
Fire, flood, power loss or theft can destroy hardware and interrupt service. This affects **availability** and, if there are no copies, the data itself.
## How the cloud helps
Google Cloud is organised into regions and zones, which are separate physical locations. Running a workload across several zones, or keeping backups and a recovery copy in another region, means one damaged building does not end the service. Google also operates and secures the facilities themselves under the shared responsibility model, so the customer no longer maintains a building.
## Software controls do not fix hardware loss
Authentication, firewalls and encryption protect against attackers, not against water or fire.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Multi-factor authentication:** this protects accounts from misuse and has no effect on whether a building floods.
- ✗ **B. Edge firewall:** a firewall filters network traffic and cannot stop physical damage to equipment.
- ✓ **C. Separate locations (correct):** spreading workloads and backups over zones or regions means one site's damage leaves another running, which directly answers the physical-damage risk.
- ✗ **D. Encryption at rest:** encryption keeps stolen data unreadable, but an encrypted disk destroyed by water is still destroyed.

## Key idea
Reduce physical-damage risk with geographic redundancy, using multiple zones, regions and backups.
Q008754:
## Attacks on LLMs
Large language models bring their own threats. The exam lists LLM attacks as one of the threats a cloud leader should recognise.
- **Prompt injection**: input written to override or bypass the instructions the application gave the model, so it reveals information or does something unintended.
- **Sensitive data disclosure**: the model reveals confidential data from its prompt, context or training.
- **Poisoning**: tampering with the data used to train or ground a model.
## Business implications
A chatbot with access to internal documents can leak them, give harmful answers in the company's name, or take unwanted actions if it can call tools.
## Common defences
Screen prompts and responses, restrict the data and actions the application can reach, and monitor for abuse. Google Cloud products such as Model Armor exist for this purpose, but the tested idea is recognising the threat.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. DDoS:** a denial of service aims to exhaust capacity, but this is a single crafted request seeking content.
- ✗ **B. Physical attack:** the user is typing into a public chat window and has no physical access to anything.
- ✗ **C. Cryptomining:** mining abuses compute for profit, and answering a question is the ordinary use of the model.
- ✓ **D. Prompt injection (correct):** the user's input tries to override the model's instructions to expose hidden data, a risk specific to LLM applications.

## Key idea
Prompt injection = crafted input that overrides an LLM's instructions to leak data or misbehave.
Q008755:
## Shared responsibility model
In the shared responsibility model, the cloud provider and the customer each own part of security. The split depends on the service model.
- **IaaS** (such as Compute Engine VMs): the provider is responsible for the underlying infrastructure and physical security. The customer is responsible for most of the rest: guest operating system, applications, data and access.
- **PaaS**: the provider takes on more, and responsibility for application-level controls and IAM is shared. The customer remains responsible for data security.
- **SaaS**: the provider owns most of the security work. The customer remains responsible for access controls and the data it chooses to store in the application.
## The pattern
The more managed the service, the less the customer has to secure, but the data and who can access it always stay the customer's concern.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Customer responsible for everything:** the provider is always responsible for the physical facilities and underlying infrastructure of the cloud.
- ✓ **B. Customer secures more in IaaS (correct):** with virtual machines the company runs the operating system, database and data protection, while with SaaS Google carries most of the load and the company handles access and its data.
- ✗ **C. Google fully responsible:** the customer always keeps responsibility for its data and access, whatever the service model.
- ✗ **D. Reversed roles:** in IaaS the customer manages the guest operating system and database, and in SaaS the provider operates the servers.

## Key idea
The more managed the service, the more the provider secures; the customer always owns its data and access.
Q008756:
## From shared responsibility to shared fate
The shared responsibility model says which security tasks belong to the provider and which to the customer. Google believes this stops short of helping customers reach better security outcomes, because the model can be hard to apply and customers can be left to work out the right configuration alone.
**Shared fate** builds on it and treats the relationship as an ongoing partnership. Google builds and runs a trusted platform and also:
- gives best-practice guidance and secured, attested infrastructure code, such as a secured landing zone;
- is clear and opinionated about recommended security settings;
- releases solutions that combine services to solve hard security problems;
- helps customers quantify and manage risk through cyber insurance options, using its Risk Protection Program.
## Business value
Customers who are not security experts start from a secure design instead of building one from scratch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One legal entity:** shared fate is a security partnership approach and does not merge the companies or transfer all liability.
- ✗ **B. No duty beyond hardware:** shared responsibility already gives Google more than hardware, and shared fate adds guidance on top.
- ✗ **C. Customer takes over all tasks:** the opposite of the idea, since shared fate adds more provider involvement.
- ✓ **D. Partnership beyond the boundary (correct):** shared fate keeps the responsibility split but adds Google's active help, such as blueprints, recommended settings and risk tools.

## Key idea
Shared fate = shared responsibility plus Google actively helping customers secure their workloads.
Q008757:
## Cloud versus on-premises security
Google's cloud security guidance makes two points.
- The cloud is **no more or less secure** than on-premises security by itself. How secure either one is depends on design, operation and configuration.
- Leading providers offer secure-by-design infrastructure and layered security built into the platform, from zero-trust network design and identity management to multi-factor authentication, encryption and continuous logging, and can automate security at large scale.
## Where responsibilities differ
- **On premises**: the company owns everything, including buildings, power, hardware, network, software and data.
- **Cloud**: the provider owns the facilities and underlying infrastructure, and the customer secures what it runs and puts in the cloud (identity, data, configuration).
## Challenge in the cloud
Visibility is different, since resources run outside your own network, and misconfiguration is a common cause of breaches.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No customer duties:** shared responsibility always leaves the customer with data, identity and configuration.
- ✗ **B. No policies needed:** the customer sets policies for who accesses its data, and the provider does not decide it.
- ✓ **C. Different ownership (correct):** on premises the company runs facilities and the full stack, while the cloud provider takes the physical layer and infrastructure.
- ✗ **D. No logging or MFA on premises:** these controls can be implemented on premises as well, so it is not a cloud-only capability.
- ✓ **E. Neither inherently safer (correct):** Google states cloud is no more or less secure than on premises and credits provider-built layered security.

## Key idea
Cloud is not inherently more or less secure; the difference is who owns which layer.
Q008758:
## The confidentiality, integrity, availability triad
Cloud security aims to protect three properties of data and systems.
- **Confidentiality**: only authorized people and systems can read data. Encryption and access control support it.
- **Integrity**: data stays accurate and unaltered except by authorized changes. Hashes, change tracking, audit logs and restricted write access support it.
- **Availability**: systems and data can be used when needed. Redundancy, backups and DDoS protection support it.
## Reading the scenario
Nothing leaked (confidentiality is intact) and the database stayed online (availability is intact). The problem is that the values were changed, so the records can no longer be trusted: integrity.
## Business implication
Wrong billing amounts cause financial loss, disputes and regulatory trouble.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Confidentiality:** the scenario says no data leaked, so unauthorized reading did not occur.
- ✓ **B. Integrity (correct):** policy amounts were modified without proper authority, so the data is no longer trustworthy even though it was neither exposed nor offline.
- ✗ **C. Compliance:** compliance means meeting laws or standards, and the scenario does not describe any provider losing certifications, only altered data.
- ✗ **D. Availability:** the database stayed online, so people could still reach it.

## Key idea
Integrity = data stays accurate and unaltered by unauthorized changes.
Q008759:
## Control and compliance in a cloud security model
- **Control** is the customer's ability to decide how its resources are secured and used: who has access, where data is located, what keys protect it and which settings apply. Moving to the cloud should not mean giving this up.
- **Compliance** is meeting the requirements of laws, regulations and industry standards (for example HIPAA for health data or PCI DSS for payment cards) and being able to show evidence to auditors.
## How they connect
Good control supplies the evidence for compliance. Under shared responsibility, the provider's certifications and infrastructure controls (inherited controls) can be part of the customer's evidence, while the customer is still responsible for its own configuration and data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Control and compliance (correct):** control is the company's own say over access and data location, and compliance is following and proving adherence to external rules.
- ✗ **B. Swapped terms:** this reverses the definitions, because compliance is about external rules and control is about the company's own decisions.
- ✗ **C. Confidentiality and resilience:** confidentiality keeps data private and resilience is the ability to withstand and recover from attacks, neither of which means regulatory adherence.
- ✗ **D. Availability and integrity:** those are properties of the data and systems (usable, unaltered), not terms for governing access or satisfying regulators.

## Key idea
Control = your decisions over access and data; compliance = meeting and proving external rules.
Q008760:
## Data loss prevention (DLP)
**Data loss prevention** is a set of tools and practices that find sensitive data, classify it, and help prevent it from being exposed or leaving the organization. In Google's cloud security guidance, DLP provides capabilities to automatically discover, classify and de-identify regulated cloud data.
## Business value
- Know where regulated data such as personal, health or payment information lives.
- Mask or remove it before it is shared or used for analytics or AI.
- Support compliance and reduce breach impact.
## Reading the scenario
The problem is not traffic or recovery; it is not knowing where sensitive data sits. Discovering and classifying it is what DLP does. Sensitive Data Protection is the Google Cloud service for this.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Data loss prevention (correct):** it scans for sensitive items such as ID numbers and diagnoses, classifies them and can mask or de-identify them.
- ✗ **B. Firewall:** a firewall controls network traffic by rules and does not inspect stored files for sensitive content.
- ✗ **C. Cyber resilience:** it is about withstanding and recovering from attacks, and it does not locate or label sensitive data.
- ✗ **D. Decryption:** decryption only makes encrypted data readable with the right key and does not search for sensitive content.

## Key idea
DLP finds, classifies and protects sensitive data so it does not leak.
Q008761:
## Least privilege and privileged access
- **Least privilege**: users, applications and partners receive only the minimum access required to do their job, and nothing more. If an account is stolen or misused, the damage is limited to what that account could do.
- **Privileged access**: accounts with powerful rights, such as administrators who can change settings, read all data or grant access to others. They are high-value targets and need stronger controls.
## Practices
- Grant narrow, role-based permissions and review them regularly.
- Use multi-factor authentication, time-limited elevation and logging for privileged accounts.
- Avoid shared accounts, because no one can then be held accountable.
In Google Cloud, IAM roles are the mechanism, but the idea applies to any environment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Self-approval:** it removes the check that stops misuse, so it weakens control of privileged access.
- ✗ **B. Same broad role for all:** this is the opposite of least privilege and makes every stolen account dangerous.
- ✓ **C. Protect privileged accounts (correct):** stronger authentication, limited use and monitoring address the high risk that powerful accounts carry.
- ✗ **D. Shared password:** a shared credential cannot be traced to a person and is easy to leak.
- ✓ **E. Minimum necessary permissions (correct):** narrowing access and removing unneeded rights limits what a compromised account can do.

## Key idea
Least privilege = minimum access needed; privileged accounts need extra protection.
Q008762:
## Zero-trust architecture
Google defines zero trust as a security model based on the idea that no person or device should be trusted by default, even if already inside the organization's network. It removes implicit trust by enforcing strict authentication and authorization throughout the network, not just at a perimeter. Every request is treated as if it comes from an untrusted network until it has been inspected, authenticated and verified.
## Why it matters
In a perimeter model, an attacker who gets in can move freely (lateral movement). With zero trust:
- policies depend on identity, device, location and context, and are re-assessed regularly;
- resources are inaccessible by default;
- the network is divided into small segments (micro-segmentation);
- traffic is logged and analyzed for signs of compromise.
Google's own implementation of this idea is called BeyondCorp.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One-time perimeter check:** zero trust continuously validates, and a single login does not give lasting trust.
- ✓ **B. Untrusted until verified (correct):** access is granted per request based on identity and context, which stops a stolen connection from giving free movement.
- ✗ **C. Trust inside, check outside:** this is the traditional perimeter model that zero trust replaces.
- ✗ **D. Remove internal checks:** zero trust adds checks at every access point, so removing internal controls is the opposite.

## Key idea
Zero trust = never grant implicit trust, and verify every request by identity and context.
Q008763:
## Two terms
- **Security by default** (secure by default or by design): protections are part of the platform from the start and do not depend on the customer remembering to enable them. For example, Google Cloud encrypts customer data at rest by default, and Google describes its infrastructure as secure by design with layered security built in.
- **Security posture**: the overall strength and state of an organization's security: its policies, controls, configurations, visibility into assets and ability to detect and respond to threats. A posture can be assessed, scored and improved over time.
This definition of posture is the generic industry meaning.
## Why executives care
Defaults reduce the chance of human error such as leaving encryption off, and posture assessments show where to invest.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Deleting data and report speed:** data deletion is a retention practice, and reporting speed is one small part of response, not the whole posture.
- ✗ **B. Customer must switch on:** that is the opposite of by default, and certifications are evidence for compliance, not the posture itself.
- ✗ **C. Only the firewall and staff count:** a single control is not a default security model and team size does not measure posture.
- ✓ **D. Built-in protection and overall state (correct):** defaults mean the safe choice is already in place, and posture describes how well protected the organization currently is.

## Key idea
Security by default = protection built in; security posture = the overall state of security.
Q008764:
## Cyber resilience
**Cyber resilience** is the ability of an organization to prepare for, withstand, respond to and recover from cyber incidents while continuing to deliver its critical services. It accepts that some attacks will get through and asks how fast and how well the business recovers.
This is the generic industry definition.
## What it includes
- **Prevent**: good configuration, access control and training.
- **Detect**: monitoring and threat intelligence.
- **Respond**: a rehearsed incident plan.
- **Recover**: tested, protected backups and redundancy to restore operations.
## Business view
Resilience protects revenue and reputation. For ransomware, strong recovery means the organization does not have to rely on the attacker to get its data back.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data loss prevention:** DLP helps protect sensitive data but does not guarantee that attacks fail or provide recovery.
- ✓ **B. Cyber resilience (correct):** it plans for success of an attack as well as prevention, with detection, response and recovery so service continues.
- ✗ **C. Zero trust:** zero trust removes implicit trust everywhere, which is the opposite of a single trusted zone, and no approach stops every attack.
- ✗ **D. Security by default:** it is about built-in protection of platforms, and it is not limited to locks nor does it exclude customers.

## Key idea
Cyber resilience = prepare, detect, respond and recover so the business keeps running through attacks.
Q008765:
## The three states of data
Encryption protects data in different states.
- **At rest**: stored on disks, databases or object storage. Google Cloud encrypts customer data at rest by default.
- **In transit**: moving between locations, for example from a user to a service or between services. Encryption on the network keeps eavesdroppers from reading it.
- **In use**: being processed in memory by a CPU. Data usually has to be decrypted to be computed on, so this is the gap that remains.
## Protecting data in use
Google's encryption page says confidential computing encrypts data in use with Confidential VMs and Confidential GKE Nodes. This helps organizations that process highly sensitive data, such as in regulated industries or shared environments.
## Reading the scenario
Stored and transmitted data are already encrypted, so the remaining state is data in use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Backups:** backups are data at rest and are covered by encryption at rest, so they are not a separate unprotected state.
- ✗ **B. At rest:** the CISO already encrypted stored data, and encryption at rest does not depend on queries running.
- ✗ **C. In transit:** the stem states the connections are encrypted, so that state is covered.
- ✓ **D. Data in use (correct):** the query processes data in memory, where it is normally readable, so confidential computing is the control that covers this state.

## Key idea
At rest and in transit are common; data in use is the one confidential computing protects.
Q008766:
## Three separate questions
- **Authentication**: who are you? Proof of identity with something you know (password), have (phone or security key) or are (biometrics).
- **Authorization**: what are you allowed to do? In Google Cloud, Identity and Access Management (IAM) gives specific roles to identities on specific resources.
- **Auditing**: what did you do? Logs record who did what, where and when, so the organization can investigate and demonstrate compliance.
## Multi-factor authentication
**Multi-factor authentication (MFA)**, including 2-step verification, requires two or more different kinds of proof. A stolen password alone is then not enough, which blunts phishing.
## Reading the scenario
Password plus phone code is authentication; the access that is granted is authorization; the later record of who opened the reports is auditing.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Swapped:** authorization decides permissions, not identity, and authentication does not record activity.
- ✗ **B. Auditing and authentication:** auditing looks back at records and does not verify sign-ins, and authentication does not set permissions.
- ✓ **C. Authentication, authorization and auditing (correct):** the sign-in proves identity, permissions decide what may be opened, and the log review is auditing.
- ✗ **D. Encryption and decryption:** these protect data confidentiality and are not identity or permission steps.

## Key idea
Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you may do; auditing = what you did.
Q008767:
## Security operations (SecOps) terms
Security operations is the work of monitoring, detecting and responding to threats. Three terms appear often.
- **Security posture**: the overall state of defences and visibility, assessed before anything happens.
- **Threat intelligence**: information about who attackers are, what they target, how they operate and what signs they leave (such as malicious addresses or file signatures). ## CapEx and OpEx
- **Capital expenditure (CapEx)** is money spent up front to acquire assets such as servers, storage arrays and network gear. The cost is usually spread over the asset's useful life through depreciation.
- **Operational expenditure (OpEx)** is money spent as the business operates, for example power, support contracts or services consumed each month.
Google's Well-Architected Framework describes the difference: on-premises IT includes both CapEx and OpEx, with acquired hardware and software depreciated over its operating life, while in the cloud the cost of most resources is treated as OpEx and is incurred as the resources are consumed. (The CapEx/OpEx definitions are generally accepted accounting terms; the cloud-side statement comes from the Well-Architected cost pillar.)
## Why a CFO cares
- No large purchase has to be approved years before demand is known.
- Cost follows usage, so a quiet quarter costs less than a busy one.

- ✗ **B. Still CapEx:** Google owns and runs the underlying servers and network, so the manufacturer has no hardware purchase to capitalize for these workloads.
- ✗ **C. Cost eliminated:** the company still pays for what it uses. The change is in how and when it pays, not that the cost disappears.
- ✗ **D. OpEx to CapEx:** this reverses the shift. Cloud resources are generally billed as they are consumed, not paid up front and depreciated.

## Key idea
Moving to the cloud turns up-front hardware CapEx into consumption-based OpEx.

- **Running costs**: facilities, power, cooling, network, and the people who operate and maintain the environment.

Items that are the same in both options, or that are not costs of the infrastructure, do not change the comparison and are left out.

- ✗ **A. Expected revenue:** revenue is a benefit, not a cost of ownership. TCO compares costs, and revenue would be weighed separately in a business case.
- ✗ **B. Marketing budget:** this spend is unrelated to where the servers run and would be identical under either option, so it adds nothing to the comparison.
- ✗ **C. Identical licence fee:** a cost that is the same under both options does not distinguish them, so it does not change the TCO difference between the options.

- ✓ **E. Facilities, power and cooling (correct):** these recurring costs come with owning servers and are missing from a purchase-price-only comparison, so they belong in the on-premises TCO.

TCO counts every cost of owning and operating the infrastructure, not only the purchase price.

- **Technology**: the tools that provide visibility and automation, for example billing reports, budgets with alerts, and dashboards.
(The three-way grouping is a common change-management framing; the cost pillar's core principles of aligning spend with value, a culture of cost awareness and continuous optimization map onto it.)
## Sorting the examples
A recurring review with agreed actions is a routine, so it is process. Training and culture are people. Dashboards and alerts are tools, so technology.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Building a custom billing tool:** this is also technology, and it duplicates cost reports that Google Cloud already provides, so it is not an example of process.
- ✓ **B. Monthly review with forecasts and follow-ups (correct):** a repeatable routine that links spending to plans is the process element.
- ✗ **C. Dashboards and alert emails:** these are tools that deliver visibility, so they belong to technology.
- ✗ **D. Training and culture:** building skills and a sense of ownership concerns people, not a routine or a tool.

## Key idea
People bring skills and ownership, process brings repeatable routines, technology brings visibility and automation.
Q008792:

Use Cloud Billing reports and the FinOps hub for continuous, shared cost visibility.
Q008793:
## The resource hierarchy
Google Cloud organizes resources in a tree:
- **Resources** such as VMs, buckets and datasets are the things you use.
- **Projects** are the base container for resources. Every resource belongs to a project.
- **Folders** group projects (and other folders), for example by department or environment.
- **Organization node** is the root, representing the company.
## Why the hierarchy helps
IAM access policies and organization policies are attached at a level of the tree and flow down, so everything below inherits them. Granting or restricting something at a folder applies to all current and future projects and folders inside it.
## Reading the scenario
One policy for many projects, including new ones, is the job of a folder. Resources are too low, billing accounts do not hold access rules, and a project cannot contain other projects.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Project as a parent:** projects hold resources and cannot contain other projects. Only folders and the organization node are parents of projects.
- ✓ **B. Folder for the division (correct):** a policy applied at the folder is inherited by every project in it, now and later, so central IT configures it once.
- ✗ **C. A billing account per project:** a billing account handles who pays, not the access and security policy of the resources, and a separate one per project multiplies administration.
- ✗ **D. Individual resources:** configuring each VM and bucket separately is the manual work the team wants to avoid and does not cover projects created later.

## Key idea
Attach policies at a folder or the organization so they are inherited by everything below.
Q008794:
## What the hierarchy gives a business
- **Access control and inheritance**: IAM allow policies and organization policies attach to organization, folder or project, and flow down. Granting a role to a team at a folder gives access to all projects in it, so there is less manual setup.
- **Security and compliance**: central teams can set guardrails once at the top, for example restrictions that apply to every project, and children inherit them.
- **Visibility and auditing**: because everything hangs under one organization node, administrators and auditors have one structure in which to see what exists and who has access.
## What it does not do
The hierarchy does not set spending limits by itself (budgets and quotas do that) and does not isolate networks automatically.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Unchangeable folder policies:** policies can be changed by users who hold the right permissions, so inheritance is not a lock.
- ✗ **B. Automatic cost limits:** the hierarchy organizes resources and policy, but spending limits come from budgets and quotas that must be set up.
- ✓ **C. Inheritance for consistent security (correct):** policies set high in the tree flow down, so security and compliance rules are applied consistently without per-project work.
- ✗ **D. No communication between projects:** projects are not network walls, and resources in different projects can communicate when allowed.
- ✓ **E. Organization-wide visibility (correct):** a single root gives administrators and auditors one structure in which to review projects, folders, resources and their access policies.

## Key idea
The hierarchy gives inherited access and policy plus organization-wide visibility for auditing.
Q008795:
## What budgets do
A Cloud Billing budget lets you track actual spend against a planned amount. You pick the scope (a billing account, projects, folders, services or labelled resources), the period and the amount, and then set **threshold rules**: when actual or forecasted cost crosses a percentage, alert emails go to the recipients you choose.
## What they do not do
Google's documentation describes alerts-only budgets: they send notifications to keep people informed and do not by default stop usage. (The documentation also mentions spend cap budgets for some services; for this exam, think of budgets as the alerting tool.) If a business wants action, a person or an automated process has to respond to the alert.
## Related tools
- **Quotas** restrict how much of a resource a project can use.
- **Reports** show where the money went.
Alerts warn, quotas limit, reports explain.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Alerts-only behaviour (correct):** threshold rules notify people as spend crosses a percentage, so nothing is shut off unless someone or an automated process acts on the alert.
- ✗ **B. Ignored for multi-service projects:** budgets can be scoped to a project, several services or the whole billing account, so nothing is ignored.
- ✗ **C. Approval needed:** threshold alerts fire automatically when spend or forecast crosses the percentage, with no approval step.
- ✗ **D. Always disables the project:** budgets do not stop usage by default, so continued running is expected behaviour, not a misconfiguration.

## Key idea
Budget thresholds notify; they do not stop spending unless someone acts.
Q008796:
## Quotas as a guardrail
Google Cloud uses quotas to maintain fairness and reduce spikes in resource use. A quota restricts how much of a Google Cloud resource a project can use, such as the number of VMs or the rate of API requests. In most cases, when you try to consume more than the quota allows, the system blocks access to the resource and the task fails. Quotas generally apply at project level.
## Business use
- They limit the damage of a mistake or compromised credentials, because consumption stops at the cap.
- Teams can ask for higher quotas through the Cloud Quotas system when there is a real need.
## Compare with other controls
- **Budget alerts** tell you after spend rises.
- **Billing reports** explain spend after it has happened.
- **Quotas** limit consumption beforehand.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Resource quota (correct):** it caps what a project can consume and blocks requests beyond that, so a runaway script or stolen credentials cannot create unlimited resources.
- ✗ **B. Invoice sign-off:** approving payment happens after the usage is already billed, so it does not stop consumption.
- ✗ **C. Larger billing account:** account size does not set limits; quotas are applied to projects and resources.
- ✗ **D. Weekly report:** a report is reviewed after the spend has occurred, and a Monday review would miss an overnight surge.

## Key idea
Quotas limit consumption in advance; budgets and reports only inform.
Q008797:
## Spot VMs
Spot VMs are virtual machines that use excess Compute Engine capacity. They have significant discounts compared with on-demand prices, but Compute Engine might stop or delete (preempt) them at any time to reclaim the capacity. Google recommends them for fault-tolerant workloads such as batch processing.
## The trade-off
- **Gain**: much lower cost for compute that would otherwise cost full price.
- **Risk**: interruption with little warning.
That trade is acceptable when the work can be split, retried and resumed, and a delay is harmless. It is not acceptable for services that must always be up.
## Reading the scenario
Independent, retryable pieces with a morning deadline are the textbook match for Spot VMs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Payment service on Spot:** an always-on customer-facing service cannot tolerate sudden reclaim, so the saving is not worth the outages.
- ✗ **B. Always-on peak fleet:** paying for peak capacity around the clock keeps the cost high and contradicts the aim of paying only for what is needed.
- ✗ **C. Cancel the nightly job:** this hurts the business to avoid a risk that the job design already tolerates.
- ✓ **D. Spot VMs for restartable batch work (correct):** interrupted pieces are simply retried, so the company gains the discount and the risk is only a short delay.

## Key idea
Spot VMs cut cost for fault-tolerant, restartable work and are a poor fit for always-on services.
Q008798:
## Obtaining scarce capacity cost-effectively
Compute Engine offers provisioning models that trade immediacy, commitment and price:
- **Standard** VMs are created immediately and run until you stop them.
- **Spot** VMs use spare capacity at a discount but can be preempted at any time.
- **Flex-start** VMs, and future reservations in calendar mode, are provisioned through the **Dynamic Workload Scheduler (DWS)**. Google describes DWS as scheduling capacity based on resource availability and helping you obtain high-demand resources such as GPUs and TPUs.
## Why it suits this case
The team can start whenever capacity becomes available, so it can queue a request for a run window instead of paying for capacity held around the clock. That keeps the cost aligned with use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Permanent maximum reservation:** it guarantees capacity but pays for it whether or not it is used, which is the idle spend the finance lead wants to avoid.
- ✓ **B. Dynamic Workload Scheduler (correct):** it provisions requested capacity when it is available and helps obtain scarce GPUs and TPUs, so the team avoids paying for hardware held idle while it waits.
- ✗ **C. Spot only:** cheap, but Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and do not queue for scarce accelerators, so a long training run could be interrupted or never start.
- ✗ **D. Buying GPUs:** this is the CapEx model the team is avoiding, and it leaves the company with idle hardware and the burden of refreshing it.

## Key idea
Dynamic Workload Scheduler lets teams obtain scarce accelerators when available without paying for idle reserved capacity.
Q008799:
## The Google Cloud Observability suite
Google Cloud Observability (formerly Cloud Operations suite, and earlier Stackdriver) groups tools that let teams understand how their systems behave:
- **Cloud Monitoring**: metrics, dashboards and alerts about performance and health.
- **Cloud Logging**: collects, stores, searches and analyzes log data.
- **Cloud Trace**: shows how a request flows through services and where latency accumulates.
- **Cloud Profiler**: a low-overhead profiler that continuously gathers CPU usage and memory allocation from production applications and attributes them to the source code.
- **Error Reporting**: aggregates application error events into groups based on root cause.
## Reading the scenario
The question is where resources are consumed in the code. Profiling answers that.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud Trace:** it shows the path and timing of a request across services, which finds slow calls between services, not the resource-hungry lines of code inside one.
- ✗ **B. Error Reporting:** it groups errors and counts them, but a slow, healthy application produces no errors to group and it does not measure resource use.
- ✓ **C. Cloud Profiler (correct):** it samples production applications with low overhead and attributes CPU and memory use to the code that causes it, which tells developers where to optimize.
- ✗ **D. Cloud Logging:** logs record events and messages. They do not attribute CPU and memory consumption to specific functions.

## Key idea
Profiler shows which code uses CPU and memory; Trace shows where a request spends time.
Q008800:
## Distributed tracing
In a system of microservices a single user action touches many services. When it is slow, averages per service can all look fine while the total is poor. **Cloud Trace** records the path of a request as a trace made of spans, so you can view latency trends, inspect individual traces and find the bottleneck.
## Observability tools compared
- Trace: where does a request spend its time across services?
- Profiler: which code inside a service uses CPU and memory?
- Error Reporting: what failures are occurring and how often?
- Logging: what happened, in detail?
- Monitoring: are metrics within expected ranges, and who should be alerted?

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Cloud Trace (correct):** it follows one request through all the services involved and shows the latency of each step, which reveals the slowest hop in the checkout path.
- ✗ **B. Error Reporting:** the stem says no errors are reported. Slowness is not an application error event, so there is nothing to group.
- ✗ **C. Weekly cost report:** cost data does not explain request latency, and the claim that slow requests mean expensive services is not true.
- ✗ **D. Cloud Profiler:** it shows resource use inside code over time, not the timing of one request across services.

## Key idea
Use Cloud Trace to find which step in a multi-service request adds the delay.
Q008801:
## Error Reporting
Error Reporting helps teams identify, prioritize and triage issues across cloud services. It aggregates individual error events, each with a timestamp, context and message, into **error groups** based on root cause. Instead of thousands of similar messages, the team sees a short list of distinct problems with counts and first-seen information. It builds on Cloud Logging, because it can find errors in log entries as well as receive them directly.
## When to use which
- Raw detail of every event: Cloud Logging.
- Categorized, counted exception types: Error Reporting.
- Slow requests: Cloud Trace.
- CPU and memory by code: Cloud Profiler.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud Profiler:** it profiles resource use, so it does not list or categorize exceptions.
- ✓ **B. Error Reporting (correct):** it groups many error events into a few root-cause groups with counts, so the manager sees which problems exist and how often they occur.
- ✗ **C. Cloud Trace:** it measures latency across a request path and does not group exception types.
- ✗ **D. Uptime checks:** they report whether a site responds, not the types and counts of exceptions inside the application.

## Key idea
Error Reporting turns a flood of error events into grouped, counted problems to triage.
Q008802:
## Monitoring vs Logging
- **Cloud Monitoring** works with metrics, which are numbers over time such as response time. It provides dashboards and **alerting policies**, which notify people or groups when a metric meets criteria you define.
- **Cloud Logging** is a real-time log-management system with storage, search and analysis. It automatically collects logs from Google Cloud resources, and applications and other systems can send logs to it.
## How they work together
Monitoring tells you that something is wrong and notifies someone. Logging provides the detail needed to explain why. Metrics are compact and good for trends and thresholds, while logs are detailed records of individual events.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Profiler and Error Reporting:** Profiler does not send threshold notifications, and Error Reporting covers application errors, not a full record of what systems did.
- ✗ **B. Swapped roles:** Logging is the event store, and charting and alerting on a metric is Monitoring's main job, so the tools are matched to the wrong needs.
- ✓ **C. Monitoring for metrics and alerts, Logging for event records (correct):** the response-time chart and notification are metric features of Cloud Monitoring, and the searchable incident record is what Cloud Logging stores.
- ✗ **D. Trace for both:** Trace records request paths and latency, and does not replace metric alerting or general log storage.

## Key idea
Monitoring watches metrics and alerts; Logging keeps the detailed event records.
Q008803:
## Operational excellence
Google's Well-Architected Framework describes operational excellence as designing, implementing and managing cloud solutions that provide value, performance, security and reliability, and as operating workloads efficiently. It relies on:
- **Automation**, which removes toil and builds guardrails around repetitive tasks.
- **Orchestration**, which coordinates complex processes.
- **Data-driven insights**, which support evidence-based decisions.
It is also cultural, encouraging continuous learning and experimentation.
## Link to DevOps and SRE
The pillar's audience includes DevOps teams (automation, CI/CD, change management) and site reliability engineers (monitoring, incident response, automation). Its principles include defining service level objectives, comprehensive monitoring, managing incidents, automating change and continuous improvement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Manual, single approver:** manual checks slow change and do not scale, which is the opposite of automating repetitive work.
- ✗ **B. Zero incidents and no monitoring:** incidents will occur, and the pillar stresses observability, incident management and learning from retrospectives.
- ✗ **C. Most expensive infrastructure:** spending more does not remove the need to operate, monitor and improve, and it ignores cost optimization.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Automation, orchestration and data-driven insight with continuous learning: this is the pillar's own description of how teams operate efficiently and improve over time.

## Key idea
Operational excellence means efficient operations through automation and data, plus continuous improvement.
Q008804:
## Reliability and high availability
- **Reliability**: Google's reliability pillar defines it as a system's ability to consistently perform its intended functions within defined conditions and maintain uninterrupted service. It is achieved through redundancy, fault-tolerant design, monitoring and automated recovery.
- **High availability (HA)**: designing so the service remains available when a component fails, usually by removing single points of failure through redundant resources. The pillar's principle is to build highly available systems through resource redundancy. (The short definition is the generally accepted one.)
- **Resilience**: part of reliability. The ability to withstand and recover from failures while maintaining performance.
## Related but different terms
- **Latency** is how long a request takes.
- **Saturation** is how full a resource is.
- **Scalability** is the ability to handle growth in load.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. High availability and reliability (correct):** staying up through a failed server or building is HA achieved by redundancy, and consistently doing what customers expect is the definition of reliability.
- ✗ **B. Latency and saturation:** these are measurements of response time and resource fullness, not goals that describe surviving failures or consistent function.
- ✗ **C. Scalability and quota:** scalability handles more load rather than surviving failures, and a quota is a consumption limit.
- ✗ **D. Reliability and CapEx:** CapEx is a spending category and has nothing to do with performing a function.

## Key idea
High availability keeps service up through failures; reliability is consistent correct performance.
Q008805:
## Building resilient systems
Google's reliability pillar lists resilience measures: multi-regional deployments, automated backups and disaster recovery. It explains that resilient systems use backups, redundancy and replication to protect data and keep it accurate and accessible.
- **Redundancy**: duplicate components or locations so no single failure takes the service down.
- **Replication**: keeping copies of data in more than one place, so a location failure does not lose records or stop access.
- **Backups**: point-in-time copies you can restore from after data loss or corruption.
- **Scalable infrastructure**: capacity that grows with demand, so load does not become a failure.
## Reading the scenario
Surviving a location failure needs redundancy, and not losing records needs replicated data and backups.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Monitoring off:** Google's reliability principles call for observability to detect failures early, so removing it increases risk.
- ✓ **B. Replication and backups (correct):** copies of the data in another location and restorable backups protect records from loss.
- ✗ **C. Fixed size and manual scaling:** it reacts only after users suffer and ignores scalable infrastructure, so overload becomes an outage.
- ✗ **D. One server, one copy:** a single point of failure that loses both availability and data if it fails.
- ✓ **E. Redundant copies across zones or regions (correct):** a failure in one location leaves other copies able to serve users, which keeps the system running.

## Key idea
Redundancy keeps the service up, replication and backups keep the data safe.
Q008806:
## Replication is not a backup
- **Replication** keeps live copies of data in more than one place. It protects availability and survives the loss of a site, but changes, including mistakes and corruption, are copied to the replica too.
- **Backups** are point-in-time copies kept separately, so you can restore the data as it was before the deletion or corruption.
Google's reliability pillar lists both under data integrity: resilient systems use backups, redundancy and replication to protect data and ensure it remains accurate and accessible. It also recommends testing recovery from data loss, because a backup you have not restored is not proven.
## Business view
Choose replication for continuity during outages and backups for recovery from human error, bugs or attacks. Many systems need both.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same thing:** they serve different purposes, and a backup would have allowed the team to restore the table.
- ✗ **B. Misconfiguration:** a replica that mirrors a delete is working as designed, so nothing was set up incorrectly.
- ✗ **C. Only for cost:** replication is for availability and durability across locations, not for reducing cost.
- ✓ **D. Replication copies mistakes (correct):** a faithful replica reproduces the deletion, so a separate point-in-time backup is what restores the table.

## Key idea
Replication guards against site failure but copies errors; backups restore earlier states.
Q008807:
## The four golden signals
The four golden signals come from Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) practice and are a common starting point for monitoring a user-facing service. (No reachable Google Cloud page defines them, so this follows the generally accepted SRE definitions.)
- **Latency**: how long it takes to serve a request.
- **Traffic**: how much demand the service receives, for example requests per second.
- **Errors**: the rate of requests that fail.
- **Saturation**: how full the service is, for example memory, CPU or queue depth relative to capacity.
## Reading the scenario
Latency is still normal and nothing is failing, but resources are near their limit. That is saturation, an early warning that lets the team add capacity before customers feel it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Latency:** response times are normal in the scenario, so latency is not what is being observed.
- ✗ **B. Errors:** the stem does not mention failed requests. Errors are counted after failure, not before.
- ✓ **C. Saturation (correct):** memory and queue depth near capacity indicate how full the service is, and give advance notice before latency and errors get worse.
- ✗ **D. Traffic:** traffic measures demand, and the observation is about how close resources are to their limits.

## Key idea
Saturation tells you how close the service is to its limits, before latency or errors appear.
Q008808:
## Measuring what users feel
Google's reliability pillar recommends defining reliability from user-experience goals. It notes that server-centric metrics such as high CPU usage do not constitute an outage if users are not affected, and it points to metrics like the success ratio of user requests.
Of the four golden signals, **latency** and **errors** are the most directly user-facing: users notice slow pages and failed requests. **Traffic** shows demand and **saturation** shows how close resources are to limits. They matter for capacity, but they are indirect.
## Practical consequence
Alerts on user-visible symptoms such as slow responses and failed requests cut false alarms from machine statistics that no customer will notice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-call headcount:** staffing is not a signal from the service and says nothing about what customers experience.
- ✗ **B. Log line volume:** more log lines do not indicate more customers or harm, and logging volume is not a golden signal.
- ✓ **C. Error rate (correct):** failed requests prevent purchases, so the error rate shows customers being harmed.
- ✗ **D. Build server saturation:** developer build machines do not serve customers, so their load does not describe customer experience.
- ✓ **E. Latency (correct):** slow responses are felt directly by customers, so alerting on latency reflects their experience.

## Key idea
Latency and errors are the user-facing golden signals; traffic and saturation support capacity decisions.
Q008809:
## SLI, SLO and SLA
These SRE terms are explained in Google Cloud's SRE fundamentals article:
- **Service level indicator (SLI)**: a direct measurement of a service's behavior, for example the frequency of successful requests or probes.
- **Service level objective (SLO)**: a precise numerical target for the SLI, such as availability. Discussions about whether the service is reliable enough are framed against the SLO.
- **Service level agreement (SLA)**: a promise to customers that the SLO meets a certain level over a period, with a consequence such as a refund or extra subscription time if it fails.
## Why the SLA is often looser
The availability level in an SLA is normally looser than the internal SLO (the article gives 99.9 percent against an internal 99.95 percent) so that the team has room to react before it breaches the contract.
## DevOps and SRE link
SRE ties reliability to business objectives. Every service should have an SLO, because without one nobody can decide whether to invest in more reliability or in faster feature delivery.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. SLI, SLO and SLA (correct):** the daily measured percentage is the indicator, the internal 99.95 percent target is the objective and the customer contract with credits is the agreement.
- ✗ **B. Also scrambled:** a measured value cannot be an objective, and the contractual promise with penalties is the SLA, not an indicator.
- ✗ **C. Scrambled mapping:** a measurement is not an agreement and a contract promise is not an objective, so each term is attached to the wrong item.
- ✗ **D. All SLAs:** only the customer-facing promise with consequences is an SLA. The measurement and the internal target have different roles.

## Key idea
SLI measures, SLO targets, SLA promises customers with consequences.
